lessons.title: Accessibility foundations: WCAG 2.2, POUR and assistive tech
lessons.summary: What accessibility means for engineers, WCAG 2.2 principles and levels, what changed in 2.2, the legal context and how assistive technologies consume your page.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Accessibility (a11y) means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and operate your product. That includes people who are blind and use a screen reader, people with low vision who zoom to 400%, people who cannot use a mouse and rely on a keyboard, switch device or voice control, people who are deaf and need captions, and people with cognitive or attention disabilities who need predictable, forgiving interfaces. It also includes the temporary and situational cases: a broken wrist, glare on a phone screen, a noisy train. For an engineer the practical definition is narrower and testable: **the page exposes correct information to assistive technology, everything works from the keyboard, and the content is perceivable without relying on one sense.** The standard that turns this into checkable rules is WCAG. The size of the gap is real. WebAIM's annual "Million" report runs automated checks on the home pages of the top one million sites; in recent years roughly 95% had detectable WCAG failures, and the same handful of problems dominate every year: low-contrast text, images without alternative text, form inputs without labels, empty links and buttons, and a missing page language. None of these are hard to fix. They are what happens when nobody owns accessibility. ## WCAG 2.2 in one picture The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are published by the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023 and is the current version. It is backwards compatible: a page that meets 2.2 also meets 2.1 and 2.0. ```text WCAG 2.2 | +-- 4 principles (POUR) | Perceivable | Operable | Understandable | Robust | +-- 13 guidelines (e.g. 1.4 Distinguishable, 2.1 Keyboard Accessible) | +-- success criteria (testable statements, each Level A, AA or AAA) | e.g. 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) -> AA | 2.1.1 Keyboard -> A | 2.5.8 Target Size (Min) -> AA (new in 2.2) | +-- "Understanding" docs and "Techniques" (non-normative how-to) ``` The success criteria are the normative part. The Understanding documents explain intent and edge cases, and the Techniques list known ways to pass (and common failures). When someone argues about whether a design passes, the Understanding page for that criterion usually settles it. ### POUR, with the criteria you will actually meet - **Perceivable**: information cannot be invisible to all of a user's senses. Text alternatives for non-text content (1.1.1, A), captions for prerecorded video (1.2.2, A), structure exposed in markup rather than only visually (1.3.1 Info and Relationships, A), not using colour as the only signal (1.4.1, A), text contrast of 4.5:1 (1.4.3, AA), content that reflows at a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport without horizontal scrolling (1.4.10, AA). - **Operable**: everything works with a keyboard (2.1.1, A) with no keyboard trap (2.1.2, A), users can skip repeated blocks (2.4.1, A), pages have titles (2.4.2, A), focus order is logical (2.4.3, A) and focus is visible (2.4.7, AA). Nothing flashes more than three times per second (2.3.1, A). - **Understandable**: the page language is declared (3.1.1, A), components behave predictably and do not change context just because they received focus (3.2.1, A), inputs have labels or instructions (3.3.2, A), errors are identified in text (3.3.1, A) with suggestions where possible (3.3.3, AA). - **Robust**: every UI component has a programmatically determinable name, role, and state/value (4.1.2, A), and status messages are announced without moving focus (4.1.3, AA). ### Levels - **A**: the minimum. Failing these blocks some users completely (no keyboard access, unlabelled controls). - **AA**: the level that laws, procurement rules and company policies almost always reference. "We target WCAG 2.2 AA" is the normal engineering commitment. - **AAA**: stricter (7:1 contrast, sign-language interpretation, no time limits). W3C itself says AAA is not recommended as a blanket requirement for whole sites because some content cannot meet it. Teams cherry-pick AAA criteria that are cheap for them. Conformance is claimed per page (and per complete process, like a checkout flow): a page conforms at AA only if it meets every A and AA criterion. ### What changed in 2.2 Nine criteria were added and one removed: - **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA**: a focused element must not be completely hidden by author content such as a sticky header or cookie banner. (2.4.12 Enhanced, AAA, requires no part of it to be hidden.) - **2.4.13 Focus Appearance, AAA**: minimum size and contrast for focus indicators. - **2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA**: anything done by dragging (sortable lists, sliders, maps) must also be possible with a single pointer without dragging, for example up/down buttons. - **2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA**: pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing, with exceptions for inline links and essential cases. (2.5.5 at AAA asks for 44 by 44.) - **3.2.6 Consistent Help, A**: help mechanisms (contact link, chat) appear in the same relative place across pages. - **3.3.7 Redundant Entry, A**: do not make users re-type information they already gave in the same process; auto-fill it or let them select it. - **3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA**: no cognitive function test (remembering a password, solving a puzzle) unless there is an alternative or assistance. Allowing paste and password managers is the usual way to pass. 3.3.9 is the AAA version. - **4.1.1 Parsing** was removed because modern browsers and assistive tech no longer depend on perfectly valid markup. WCAG 3 is in development as a W3C working draft with a different scoring model. It is not a standard yet; nothing legal references it. Know it exists, do not design to it. ## The legal context (know the shape, not every statute) You are not expected to be a lawyer in an interview, but you should know why companies care. - **United States.** The ADA predates the web and its Title III regulations do not name a technical standard for private websites, but courts have repeatedly treated inaccessible sites of public-facing businesses as discrimination, and thousands of web accessibility lawsuits are filed each year. The Department of Justice's 2024 rule for state and local governments (ADA Title II) adopts WCAG 2.1 AA with compliance dates starting in 2026. Federal agencies and their vendors fall under **Section 508**, which incorporates WCAG 2.0 AA. - **European Union.** The **European Accessibility Act** applies from 28 June 2025 to many private-sector products and services, including e-commerce, banking, e-books and transport ticketing. Its harmonised standard, EN 301 549, maps its web requirements to WCAG 2.1 AA. Public-sector bodies were already covered by the Web Accessibility Directive. - **Elsewhere.** Canada (Accessible Canada Act, Ontario's AODA), the UK (Equality Act plus public sector regulations), and many others reference WCAG AA. The practical upshot: **WCAG 2.1 AA is the floor most regulators cite, 2.2 AA is the sensible target**, and enterprise customers will ask for an accessibility conformance report (a VPAT-based ACR) before they buy B2B software. ## Assistive technology: who is on the other side Knowing how people actually use your UI is what turns rules into judgement. | Technology | Who uses it | What it needs from you | | --- | --- | --- | | Screen readers (JAWS, NVDA on Windows; VoiceOver on macOS/iOS; TalkBack on Android; Narrator) | Blind and low-vision users, some people with dyslexia | Correct roles, names, states; headings and landmarks to navigate; announcements for dynamic changes | | Screen magnifiers and browser zoom | Low-vision users | Reflow at high zoom, no clipped text, focus kept in view | | Keyboard only | Motor disabilities, power users, screen reader users | Every action reachable by Tab/arrow keys, visible focus, no traps | | Switch access and sip-and-puff | Severe motor disabilities | Keyboard operability (switch software emulates keys), generous timing | | Voice control (Voice Control on macOS/iOS, Dragon, Voice Access) | Motor disabilities, RSI | Visible label text that matches the accessible name ("Label in Name", 2.5.3) so "click Send" works | | Captions and transcripts | Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, everyone in a noisy place | Accurate captions, transcripts for audio | | OS settings: reduced motion, high contrast / forced colours, larger text | Vestibular disorders, low vision, migraine | Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, survive forced-colours mode, use relative units | WebAIM's screen reader user survey consistently shows JAWS and NVDA as the dominant desktop screen readers and VoiceOver dominant on mobile, and that most screen reader users navigate an unfamiliar page **by headings first**. That one fact justifies a lot of the semantic work in later lessons. ### How a screen reader actually reads your page ```text DOM + CSS ---> browser builds the ACCESSIBILITY TREE (role, name, state, value, relationships per node) | v platform accessibility API (UIA / IAccessible2 on Windows, NSAccessibility on macOS, AT-SPI on Linux, UIAccessibility on iOS) | v screen reader: "Search, edit text, required" + virtual cursor (browse mode) and shortcut keys: H = next heading, D = next landmark, F = next form field ``` The screen reader never sees your pixels or your CSS classes. It sees the accessibility tree. If a `div` looks like a button but has no role, name or keyboard handling, it does not exist as a button for that user. ## A worked example: the same control, broken and fixed ```tsx // Broken: looks like a button, is a div. No role, no name, no keyboard access.
setOpen(true)}>
// Fixed: native button gives role, focusability, Enter/Space activation. // The icon is decorative, the name comes from visually hidden text. ``` ```css /* Visually hidden but still in the accessibility tree */ .sr-only { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding: 0; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0, 0, 0, 0); white-space: nowrap; border: 0; } ``` Four criteria fixed in one change: 2.1.1 Keyboard, 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, 2.4.7 Focus Visible (buttons get the browser focus ring unless you remove it) and 1.1.1 Non-text Content. ## Trade-offs and how teams actually do it - **Shift left, not audit at the end.** An external audit before launch finds hundreds of issues that are expensive to retrofit into a custom component library. Accessible primitives (or a vetted headless library), lint rules (`eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y`), automated axe checks in CI and a short manual keyboard and screen reader pass per feature cost far less. - **Automated tools find only a fraction.** They are good at contrast, missing names and invalid ARIA. They cannot tell whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order makes sense, or whether a custom widget is usable. Manual testing is not optional. - **Overlays do not fix sites.** Third-party "accessibility overlay" scripts that promise one-line compliance are widely criticised by disabled users and practitioners; they cannot repair semantics in your components, and sites using them still get sued. Fix the source. - **AA everywhere, AAA selectively.** Pick AAA criteria that are cheap for your product (for example 2.5.5 larger targets on mobile, 2.4.13 a strong focus style). ## Common mistakes - Treating accessibility as "screen reader support" only, and ignoring keyboard, zoom, motion and cognitive needs. - `outline: none` with no replacement focus style. It fails 2.4.7 and makes keyboard users lose their place. - Thinking a Lighthouse score of 100 means the page is accessible. It means a set of automated rules passed. - Believing `aria-label` everywhere is "doing accessibility". Extra ARIA on top of broken semantics usually makes things worse. - Forgetting `lang` on ``: screen readers then use the wrong pronunciation rules for the whole page. - Writing for WCAG 2.0 checklists from a decade ago and missing 2.2 additions like target size and focus not obscured by sticky headers. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you know accessibility as engineering rather than a checkbox. Can you name POUR, explain A/AA/AAA, say which level matters legally, and give concrete examples of failures and fixes? Senior candidates are expected to talk about process: how to make a team ship accessible UI by default. **A 60-second answer outline ("What is WCAG and what level do you target?"):** 1. WCAG is the W3C standard; 2.2 is current, organised by four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust. 2. Testable success criteria at A, AA, AAA; AA is what laws and contracts reference (ADA case law, Section 508, the EU Accessibility Act through EN 301 549). 3. Give two concrete criteria: 4.5:1 text contrast and full keyboard operability with visible focus. 4. Mention 2.2 additions: 24 px targets, focus not hidden behind sticky headers, accessible authentication. 5. Process: accessible components, lint and axe in CI, manual keyboard and screen reader checks, because tools find only part of the issues. **Follow-ups to expect:** Why is AAA not a blanket target? What does a screen reader actually consume? How would you introduce accessibility into a team that has ignored it? What do automated tools miss?
keyPoints: WCAG 2.2 (2023) organises testable success criteria under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust
AA is the level laws and contracts cite; AAA is applied selectively, never as a blanket target
WCAG 2.2 added target size (24 px), focus not obscured, dragging alternatives and accessible authentication, and dropped Parsing
Assistive tech reads the accessibility tree, not pixels: roles, names and states are what exist for a screen reader user
Automated tools catch only part of the issues; accessible components plus manual keyboard and screen reader checks are the real process

check.q: A company wants to state a realistic accessibility target in its engineering standards. Which is the usual choice?
options: WCAG 2.2 Level A only
WCAG 2.2 Level AA
WCAG 2.2 Level AAA for every page
WCAG 3 Gold
check.why: AA is what laws, procurement rules and most policies reference. W3C does not recommend AAA as a site-wide requirement, and WCAG 3 is still a draft.

check.q: Which success criterion was added in WCAG 2.2?
options: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
4.1.1 Parsing
2.1.1 Keyboard
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
check.why: 2.5.8 (24 by 24 CSS px targets, AA) is new in 2.2. 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in 2.2; the other two date from 2.0.

The CSS class names on the element
A screenshot of the page processed with OCR
The React component tree

lessons.title: Semantics and ARIA: the accessibility tree, roles, names and states
lessons.summary: How the browser builds the accessibility tree, how accessible names are computed, which ARIA states matter and why native HTML beats ARIA almost every time.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Every element on your page gets translated into a node in the **accessibility tree**: a parallel, simplified tree the browser builds from the DOM and hands to assistive technology. Each node carries four things a screen reader cares about: - **Role**: what it is (button, link, checkbox, heading level 2, navigation landmark). - **Name**: what it is called ("Delete invoice", "Search"). - **State and properties**: its current condition (expanded, checked, disabled, invalid, selected, required). - **Value**: for inputs and ranges, the current value ("42", "Berlin"). Semantic HTML fills all four in for free. ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications, the W3C WAI-ARIA spec, currently 1.2) lets you **override or add** role, name and state when HTML has no element for what you are building. ARIA changes only what is exposed to assistive technology. It does not add behaviour, focusability, keyboard handling or styling. That single sentence explains most ARIA bugs. ## How the accessibility tree is built ```text DOM Accessibility tree ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
navigation "Main"
    list (3 items)
  • Home
    • listitem > link "Home" ...
    main

    Invoices

    heading level 1 "Invoices"
    (generic: ignored / flattened)
    (generic, no name: invisible svg
    as a control) searchbox "Search invoices" ``` Things to notice: - `div` and `span` have the `generic` role. They are flattened away unless something gives them meaning. - `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, the `hidden` attribute and `aria-hidden="true"` remove nodes (and their subtree) from the tree. `opacity: 0` and off-screen positioning do **not**. - Relationships (`for`/`id`, `aria-controls`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-labelledby`) connect nodes by id. If the id is missing or duplicated, the relationship silently breaks. You can inspect this tree directly: Chrome DevTools has an Accessibility pane per element and an optional full-tree view; Firefox has an Accessibility Inspector. Make this a habit before reaching for a screen reader. ## Roles: use the element that already has it | You want | Use | Not | | --- | --- | --- | | Something that performs an action | `
keyPoints: Every node exposes role, name, state and value; that is the contract with assistive technology
ARIA changes only what assistive tech is told; it adds no focus, keyboard handling or behaviour
Accessible name order: aria-labelledby, aria-label, native label, content (for some roles), then title as a last resort
Keep visible label text inside the accessible name so voice control works (2.5.3 Label in Name)
Never put aria-hidden on a focusable element or its ancestor; generate ids with useId to avoid broken references
interview: What is the first rule of ARIA, and when is ARIA actually the right tool?
How does the browser compute an element's accessible name?
What is the accessibility tree and how do you inspect it?
When should you use a button and when a link?

check.q: A button has visible text "Cancel" and aria-label="Close dialog". What does a screen reader announce as its name?
options: Cancel
Close dialog
Cancel, Close dialog
Nothing, because the values conflict
check.why: aria-label overrides name from content. It also breaks Label in Name: a voice control user saying "click Cancel" will not match.

check.q: What does adding role="button" to a div give you automatically?
options: Focusability with the Tab key
Enter and Space activation
Form submission when inside a form
Only the button role exposed to assistive technology
check.why: ARIA changes semantics only. Focus (tabindex), keyboard activation and submit behaviour must all be implemented by hand.

check.q: Which of these removes an element from the accessibility tree?
options: opacity: 0
aria-hidden="true"
position: absolute; left: -9999px
A width and height of 1px with overflow hidden
check.why: aria-hidden (like display:none and the hidden attribute) removes the subtree. The other techniques hide visually but stay exposed, which is how sr-only text works.

lessons.title: Keyboard and focus: tab order, roving tabindex, traps and SPA focus
lessons.summary: How tab order really works, visible focus, skip links, roving tabindex versus aria-activedescendant, correct modal focus traps and focus management on SPA route changes.
keyPoints: Tab order follows DOM order; never use positive tabindex, use 0 for custom widgets and -1 for programmatic focus targets
Composite widgets are one Tab stop with arrow keys inside, via roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant
Modals trap focus, close on Escape and return focus to the trigger; dialog.showModal() and inert do most of the work
On SPA route changes, focus the new h1 or announce the title; never leave focus on a removed element
Replace outlines with :focus-visible styles rather than removing them, and keep focus clear of sticky headers
interview: How do you handle focus when a modal dialog opens and closes?
What is roving tabindex, and how does it differ from aria-activedescendant?
How should a single-page app manage focus and announcements on route changes?
What do tabindex values 0, -1 and positive numbers do, and when do you use each?

check.q: A toolbar has 12 buttons. Following the APG keyboard model, how many Tab stops should it take?
options: 12, one per button
1, with arrow keys moving between buttons
0, toolbars are reached only via landmarks
2, one for the first and one for the last button
check.why: Composite widgets are a single Tab stop. Roving tabindex keeps one button at tabindex=0 and arrow keys move focus within.

check.q: Why is outline usually better than box-shadow for a focus indicator?
options: box-shadow is not supported on buttons
outline triggers layout and is therefore more visible
Forced-colours (high contrast) mode removes box-shadow but keeps and recolours outlines
WCAG requires the CSS outline property specifically
check.why: In Windows forced-colours mode, box shadows disappear. A real or transparent outline remains visible to those users.

check.q: After a client-side route change in an SPA, a screen reader user hears nothing. Which fix matches common practice?
options: Reload the page on every navigation
Add tabindex="0" to every paragraph on the new page
Set aria-hidden on the old content
Move focus to the new page's h1 (tabindex=-1) or announce the new title in a polite live region
check.why: Focusing the heading announces the new page and resets the Tab start point; a route announcer reading document.title is the alternative.

lessons.title: Accessible forms: labels, descriptions, errors and live validation
lessons.summary: Label association, grouping with fieldset and legend, hints via aria-describedby, aria-invalid, the error summary pattern, autocomplete and when to validate as the user types.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Forms are where accessibility failures cost money: a blind user who cannot tell which field is invalid abandons checkout; a user with a cognitive disability who loses everything on a validation error gives up on signing up. WebAIM's Million report lists missing form labels among the most common failures every year. An accessible form does five things: 1. Every control has a **programmatic label** that matches its visible label. 2. Instructions and format hints are **associated** with the field, not just placed near it. 3. Related controls are **grouped** with a name (radio groups, address blocks). 4. Errors are **identified in text**, tied to the field, announced, and easy to reach and fix. 5. The form is **forgiving**: autocomplete, paste, no needless re-entry, no timeouts that destroy work. The criteria: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A), 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (A), 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A), 3.3.1 Error Identification (A), 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA), 3.3.4 Error Prevention for legal and financial submissions (AA), 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (AA), 2.5.3 Label in Name (A), and the WCAG 2.2 additions 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A) and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (AA). ## Labels ```tsx // Best: explicit association. Clicking the label focuses the input, // which also enlarges the pointer target. // Also fine: implicit wrapping ``` What does **not** count as a label: - **Placeholder text.** It disappears when typing starts, is usually low contrast, and is not reliably used as the accessible name. It is a hint at most. - **Text next to the field** with no association. Sighted users see the relationship; the accessibility tree does not. - **`aria-label` with a different visible label.** Voice control users say what they see. When there is genuinely no visible label (a search field next to a magnifier button), `aria-label="Search"` or a visually hidden label is acceptable, but a visible label is better for everyone, including people with memory difficulties who forget what the field was for once they start typing. ### Groups ```tsx
Delivery speed
``` Screen readers announce the legend when focus enters the group ("Delivery speed, grouping, Standard 3-5 days, radio button, 1 of 2"). Without it, "Express, radio button" has no question. Use `fieldset`/`legend` for radio and checkbox groups and for repeated blocks (billing address versus shipping address). Custom groups can use `role="group"` or `role="radiogroup"` with `aria-labelledby`. ## Descriptions and hints ```tsx

At least 12 characters. Spaces are allowed.

``` `aria-describedby` makes the hint part of what is announced on focus: "Password, secure edit text, At least 12 characters. Spaces are allowed." Put hints **before** the input in visual order too, so screen magnifier users see them before they start typing. You can reference several ids: `aria-describedby="pw-hint pw-error"`. Required fields: use the native `required` attribute (exposes required state, enables browser validation if you want it) or `aria-required="true"` for custom controls. A visual asterisk needs an explanation ("Fields marked * are required") and the asterisk itself can be `aria-hidden` since the state is already announced. ## Input purpose and autocomplete `autocomplete` tokens (`name`, `email`, `tel`, `street-address`, `postal-code`, `cc-number`, `one-time-code`, `current-password`, `new-password`) let browsers and password managers fill fields. That is 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (AA): users with motor or cognitive disabilities type far less. It also helps 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication: allowing password managers and paste (never blocking paste on password or code fields) is the simplest way to avoid a "memorise and type" cognitive test. `one-time-code` lets iOS and Android offer the SMS code. ## Error messaging that works An error needs to be: **visible text** (not only a red border, which fails 1.4.1 Use of Color), **specific** ("Enter a date in the past" not "Invalid input"), **associated** with the field, **announced** when it appears, and **easy to navigate to**. ```tsx function EmailField({ error }: { error?: string }) { const id = useId(); const errorId = `${id}-error`; const hintId = `${id}-hint`; return (

We will send the receipt here.

{error && (

{error}

)}
); } ``` - `aria-invalid="true"` exposes the invalid state ("invalid entry"). Set it only after validation fails, not on an empty untouched field. - `aria-describedby` includes the error so it is read whenever the field gets focus. - `aria-errormessage` is the purpose-built ARIA attribute for this, but screen reader support has historically been patchy; `aria-describedby` is the robust choice in 2026, and some teams set both. - The icon is decorative; the word carries the meaning. ### On submit: the error summary pattern For anything longer than two or three fields, on a failed submit: 1. Render an **error summary** at the top of the form: a heading ("There is a problem") and a list of links, each pointing to the invalid field's id. 2. **Move focus to the summary** (`tabIndex={-1}`) so screen readers read it immediately and keyboard users start from it. 3. Keep **inline errors** next to each field as well. 4. Prefix the page title with "Error: " for full-page server-rendered forms so the problem is announced on load. The GOV.UK Design System documents this pattern with years of user research behind it, and it is the most cited reference for form errors. ```tsx function ErrorSummary({ errors }: { errors: { field: string; message: string }[] }) { const ref = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { if (errors.length) ref.current?.focus(); }, [errors]); if (!errors.length) return null; return (

There is a problem

    {errors.map((e) => (
  • {e.message}
    • ))}
); } ``` The alternative for short forms: on submit, move focus to the **first invalid field**. Its label, state and error are announced together. ## Live validation: when and how Validating on every keystroke is the most common way to make a form hostile. The user types the first letter of their email and is told it is invalid; a screen reader interrupts on every key. A widely used rule of thumb is **"reward early, punish late"**: ```text Field state When to validate What to do ----------------- ------------------- ---------------------------------- untouched never nothing being typed (ok) never show error (optionally show success later) on blur validate show error + aria-invalid already invalid, on each change remove the error as soon as it user is fixing it becomes valid ("reward early") submit validate all error summary or focus first error ``` Announcing errors as they appear: inline errors that appear on blur are read when the user returns to the field, via `aria-describedby`. If you want an immediate announcement, use a polite live region (lesson 5), not `role="alert"` on every field, which interrupts whatever the user is doing. Async checks ("username taken") are a good fit for a polite status message after the user pauses. Character counters: announce at thresholds ("20 characters left") through a polite live region, not on every keystroke. ## Server Actions and progressive enhancement In a Next.js or React 19 app, form validation often happens on the server. Make the returned errors render the same accessible markup, and keep native `name` attributes so the form also works before hydration. Re-populate the fields with the submitted values (3.3.7 Redundant Entry, and basic decency). With `useActionState`, return a field-error map and move focus to the summary in an effect when it changes. Whether to use native browser validation (`required`, `type="email"`, `:user-invalid`) is a trade-off: native bubbles are announced reasonably well and need no code, but you cannot style or word them consistently, and they appear one at a time. Many teams add `noValidate` to the form and render their own messages while keeping `required` and types for semantics and mobile keyboards. ## Trade-offs and edge cases - **Disabled submit buttons until the form is valid** hide the reason. Users (especially screen reader users, who may not find the disabled button) do not know what is wrong. Keep the button enabled and show errors on submit. - **Custom selects and date pickers**: the native control is almost always more accessible on mobile. If you build a custom one, follow the APG combobox or grid pattern and test it on real assistive tech. - **Time limits**: 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (A) requires warning and the ability to extend session timeouts that would lose form data. - **Legal and financial submissions** (3.3.4 AA): let users review, correct, or reverse before final submission. ## Common mistakes and debugging - Labels using `for` that points to a non-existent or duplicated id (copy-pasted components). - Errors shown only as red borders or only via a toast that disappears. - `aria-invalid="false"` sprinkled everywhere (harmless but noise) or `aria-invalid="true"` on fields that were never touched. - Hints placed after the input or in a tooltip that only appears on hover. - `role="alert"` on every inline error, causing a storm of interruptions on submit. - Blocking paste on email confirmation or password fields. Debugging: in DevTools' accessibility pane, check each input's computed name and description. With a screen reader, Tab through the form, submit it empty, and listen: can you tell what went wrong and get to it? ## In the interview **What they probe:** concrete markup knowledge (label association, fieldset/legend, describedby, aria-invalid) and judgement about when to validate and how to announce. A common exercise: "Here is a sign-up form; make it accessible." **Model 60-second answer ("How do you make form errors accessible?"):** 1. Errors are text, specific, and visible next to the field, never colour alone. 2. Field gets `aria-invalid="true"` and `aria-describedby` pointing at the error (plus its hint). 3. On submit, an error summary with links to each field receives focus; for short forms focus the first invalid field. 4. Validate on blur or submit, clear errors as soon as they are fixed; do not shout on every keystroke. 5. Keep the submit button enabled, preserve entered values, and support autocomplete and paste. **Follow-ups:** Why is placeholder not a label? `aria-errormessage` versus `aria-describedby`? How do you announce async validation? Native validation or custom?
keyPoints: Every control needs a programmatic label matching its visible text; placeholder is not a label
Group radios and checkboxes with fieldset and legend; attach hints and errors with aria-describedby
Errors are specific text tied to the field with aria-invalid, never colour alone
On submit, focus an error summary with links to fields (or the first invalid field on short forms)
Reward early, punish late: validate on blur or submit, clear errors as soon as they are fixed
interview: How do you make form validation errors accessible?
Why is a placeholder not a substitute for a label, and how do you label form controls correctly?
When should a form validate as the user types, and how should errors be announced?

check.q: Which approach correctly ties an inline error message to its input for screen readers?
options: Give the input a red border and an error icon
Set aria-invalid="true" and reference the error element's id in aria-describedby
Put the error text in the input's placeholder
Add role="alert" to every field wrapper permanently
check.why: aria-invalid exposes the state and aria-describedby makes the error part of what is announced on focus. Colour alone fails 1.4.1.

check.q: Why do many accessibility practitioners advise against disabling the submit button until a form is valid?
options: Disabled buttons cannot be styled
Disabled buttons fail the contrast criterion automatically
Users get no explanation of what is wrong, and disabled buttons are skipped by Tab so they may not even be found
Browsers submit the form anyway
check.why: Keeping the button enabled and showing specific errors on submit tells users what to fix; a silent disabled button does not.

check.q: What does autocomplete="email" on an input help satisfy?
options: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose, letting browsers and assistive tools fill the field
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
2.4.7 Focus Visible
4.1.3 Status Messages
check.why: Autocomplete tokens make the purpose machine-readable, reducing typing for users with motor and cognitive disabilities.

lessons.title: Dynamic content: live regions, route announcements, loading states and toasts
lessons.summary: Why dynamic changes are silent to screen readers, how live regions and status roles work, an app-level announcer, route announcements, loading states and accessible toasts.
lessons.body:
## The core idea A sighted user notices when "Saved" appears in the corner, a cart badge changes from 2 to 3, or a spinner turns into results. A screen reader user is reading wherever their virtual cursor or focus is, and hears nothing about changes elsewhere on the page unless you tell the screen reader to speak. There are exactly two ways to communicate a change: 1. **Move focus** to the new content. Use this when the user must act on it: a dialog opened, a new page loaded, an error summary appeared. 2. **Announce it** through a **live region** without moving focus. Use this for status: "3 results", "Message sent", "Saving...", "Item added to cart". WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) requires the second: status messages that do not receive focus must be programmatically determinable through role or properties so assistive tech can present them. ## How live regions work A live region is an element whose content changes the screen reader watches and speaks. ```text 1. Page loads; the live region element is already in the DOM (often empty)
2. Screen reader / browser registers it as a live region 3. Your code changes its text content "Saved" -> browser fires a change event in the a11y API 4. Screen reader queues the text: polite -> spoken when the user is idle (after current speech) assertive -> may interrupt current speech 5. User hears "Saved" while focus stays where it was ``` The attributes: - `aria-live="polite"`: announce when idle. The default choice for almost everything. - `aria-live="assertive"`: interrupt. Reserve for time-critical, important messages (session about to expire, connection lost, payment failed). - `aria-atomic="true"`: read the whole region, not just the changed node. Useful when the region is "Cart: 3 items" and only the number changes. - `aria-relevant`: which kinds of changes count (additions, removals, text). Rarely needed and inconsistently supported; leave it at the default. - `aria-busy="true"`: tells AT that a region is being updated and to wait; set it back to false when done. The roles with implied live behaviour: | Role | Implicit | Use for | | --- | --- | --- | | `status` | polite, atomic | Results counts, "Saved", progress text | | `alert` | assertive, atomic | Errors needing immediate attention | | `log` | polite, additions | Chat messages, activity feeds | | `timer` | off | Countdown clocks (no automatic announcements) | | `marquee` | off | Non-essential changing info like tickers | | `progressbar` | not live | Pair with a status message at milestones | `` has an implicit `status` role in the HTML-AAM mapping, which makes it a neat element for calculation results, though support for its live behaviour has historically varied, so many teams still add `role="status"` explicitly. ## The rules that make announcements reliable 1. **The region must exist before the content changes.** Rendering `
Saved
` from nothing at the moment you want to announce is the number one reason announcements do not happen. Screen readers have to register the region first. (`role="alert"` injected with content is more forgiving in practice, but do not rely on it.) 2. **Change the text, not the attributes.** Toggling `aria-live` on an existing element is unreliable. 3. **Repeat messages need a change.** Announcing "Copied" twice in a row may be ignored if the text did not change. Clear the region and set the text again after a short delay, or append an invisible counter. 4. **Keep messages short and complete.** "3 results for 'shoes'" not the entire result list. 5. **Do not put focusable content or long structured content** in a live region; announcements are plain speech. 6. **Do not over-announce.** Every keystroke in a search box should not trigger "Loading... 42 results... Loading... 40 results". Debounce. A reusable announcer is the standard approach in apps: ```tsx // One pair of global regions, mounted once in the root layout const AnnouncerContext = createContext<(msg: string, mode?: "polite" | "assertive") => void>(() => {}); export function AnnouncerProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const [polite, setPolite] = useState(""); const [assertive, setAssertive] = useState(""); const announce = useCallback((msg: string, mode: "polite" | "assertive" = "polite") => { const set = mode === "polite" ? setPolite : setAssertive; set(""); // clear so repeats are re-read setTimeout(() => set(msg), 100); }, []); return ( {children}
{polite}
{assertive}
 ); } export const useAnnounce = () => useContext(AnnouncerContext); ``` ```tsx // Usage: filter results const announce = useAnnounce(); useEffect(() => { if (!isFetching) announce(`${results.length} results`); }, [isFetching, results.length, announce]); ``` React Aria ships a similar `announce` utility in `@react-aria/live-announcer`, and many design systems have one. Centralising it avoids dozens of competing regions. ## Route change announcements Covered from the focus side in the keyboard lesson; from the announcement side: - Next.js includes a route announcer: on client-side navigation it announces the page via a visually hidden live region, using `document.title` first, then the first `h1`, then the pathname. That means **unique, descriptive titles per page** (set via the Metadata API) are what screen reader users hear. - React Router, Vue Router and others do not announce by default; you add focus management or an announcer. - Pick one strategy (focus the `h1` or announce). Doing both can produce double announcements. ## Loading states A spinner is a picture. Without text it communicates nothing to a screen reader user, and if the content area is replaced by a skeleton, they may be reading something that just vanished. ```tsx function Results({ query }: { query: string }) { const { data, isPending } = useSearch(query); return (

Results

{isPending ? ( ) : ( )}

{isPending ? "Loading results" : `${data.length} results for ${query}`}

); } ``` Guidance: - Announce the **start** only if loading may take noticeable time (more than about a second); always announce the **outcome** ("12 results", "No results", "Could not load, try again"). - Skeleton screens should be `aria-hidden`; the status text carries the meaning. - Buttons that start an action: keep focus on the button, set it to a busy state ("Saving..." as text, or `aria-disabled` while busy) and announce completion. Swapping the button for a spinner destroys focus. - For Suspense boundaries and streaming server rendering, the fallback is content like any other: give it a status message, and when the real content streams in, focus stays put unless the user needs to act on it. - Infinite scroll: announce "20 more results loaded" and make sure keyboard users can reach the footer (or offer a "Load more" button, which is generally more accessible than automatic infinite scroll). ## Toasts and notifications Toasts are among the most broken components on the web: - They appear far from focus, so screen reader users miss them unless they are in a live region. - They disappear after a few seconds, which may be before a screen reader finishes the current utterance or before a low-vision user who zooms in has panned to them. 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable applies when content is time-limited. - They often contain actions ("Undo") that keyboard users cannot reach in time. A defensible toast design: ```text - Mounted inside a persistent polite live region (role="status"), errors in an assertive region (role="alert"). - Message text is complete on its own ("Message archived"). - No essential information only in a toast; important outcomes also appear in the page (e.g. the archived item disappears from the list). - Auto-dismiss pauses on hover and focus; long enough to read (5-10 s+), or no auto-dismiss for messages with actions. - Actions are reachable: a keyboard shortcut (e.g. F8 to jump to the notification region, Radix Toast's default) or the action is duplicated elsewhere ("Undo" also available in the item's menu). - Never move focus to a toast automatically. ``` For truly urgent interruptions that require a decision, use an alert dialog (`role="alertdialog"`), which takes focus, rather than a toast. ## Trade-offs - **Assertive versus polite**: assertive messages interrupt and can cut off what the user was hearing. Overusing them is like a colleague who shouts every update. - **Live region versus focus move**: focus moves are definitive but disruptive. Status messages are gentle but missable. If the user must respond, move focus; if it is information, announce. - **Screen reader variance**: NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver differ in how they queue and de-duplicate announcements, and VoiceOver on iOS is particularly picky about regions added late. Test on at least two. - **Verbosity**: in a real-time dashboard, announcing every update makes the page unusable. Batch ("5 new alerts"), throttle, or let the user opt in. ## Common mistakes and debugging - Live region rendered conditionally together with its message (never registered). - Live region inside an element that is `display: none` or `aria-hidden`. - Using `aria-live` on a large container that re-renders entirely, causing the whole region to be read on every change. - Two announcers on the page saying the same thing (library toaster plus your own). - Loading text announced but never the result. - Chat apps marking the whole message list `aria-live="assertive"`: every new message interrupts typing. Use `role="log"` (polite). Debugging: Chrome's accessibility pane shows live region properties on a node. Then turn on a screen reader, trigger the change, and listen; NVDA's speech viewer (in the tools menu) shows a text log of everything spoken, which is the best way to see duplicates or missing announcements. VoiceOver has a caption panel that does the same. ## In the interview **What they probe:** do you know that dynamic changes are silent by default, the difference between polite and assertive, why the region must pre-exist, and when to move focus instead? Toasts and loading states are common follow-up scenarios. **Model 60-second answer ("How do you make dynamic content changes accessible?"):** 1. Decide: must the user act? Move focus. Is it status? Announce it. 2. Announce with a live region present in the DOM before the change: `role="status"` (polite) by default, `role="alert"` for urgent errors. 3. A single app-level announcer, clear-then-set so repeats are read, debounced for search-as-you-type. 4. Loading: busy state plus "Loading" text if slow, always announce the result or the error. 5. Toasts: in a live region, long enough to read, pause on focus, never the only place important information or actions live. **Follow-ups:** Why did my announcement not fire? How do route announcements work in Next.js? How do you make a chat log accessible? What is `aria-atomic` for?
keyPoints: Changes outside focus are silent unless you move focus (user must act) or announce via a live region (status)
The live region must exist in the DOM before its text changes; change text, not attributes
Polite (role=status) is the default; assertive (role=alert) only for urgent errors
Loading states need text: announce slow starts and always announce the outcome
Toasts live in a live region, last long enough, pause on focus and never hold the only copy of important info
interview: How do you announce dynamic content changes to screen reader users?
What is the difference between aria-live polite and assertive, and why might an announcement not fire?
How would you make a toast notification system accessible?

check.q:
A developer renders
Saved
only at the moment the save completes, and nothing is announced. What is the most likely cause?
options: role="status" is assertive and was suppressed
The live region did not exist before its content was set, so the screen reader never registered it
Status messages require aria-hidden="true"
The text must be longer than 10 characters
check.why: Screen readers watch regions they already know about. Mount the empty region early and change its text.

check.q: Which is the best choice for announcing "12 results" after a filter change?
options: Move focus to the first result
role="alert" on the results list
A polite live region (role="status") with a short text message
aria-live="assertive" on the whole page
check.why: It is status information the user does not need to act on immediately, so polite announcement without moving focus fits 4.1.3.

check.q: What is role="log" designed for?
options: Debug output that should be hidden from users
Error messages that must interrupt the user
Countdown timers
Sequential additions such as chat messages, announced politely
check.why: log is a polite live region for appended content like chat or activity feeds; assertive chat logs interrupt constantly.

lessons.title: Colour, motion and media: contrast, colour-only meaning, alt text and captions
lessons.summary: WCAG contrast ratios for text and UI, never relying on colour alone, forced colours, prefers-reduced-motion, alt text decisions and captions, transcripts and audio description.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
The Perceivable principle says information must reach users through at least one sense they have. In practice this lesson covers four areas engineers own:

1. **Contrast**: text and interface parts must stand out from their background.
2. **Colour as the only signal**: red/green status, links distinguished only by colour, charts with colour-coded series.
3. **Motion**: animation can cause nausea and vertigo for people with vestibular disorders, and flashing can trigger seizures.
4. **Media and images**: alternative text for images, captions and transcripts for audio and video.

These are the most common failures in the wild. Low-contrast text tops the WebAIM Million list every year, on the large majority of home pages, and missing image alternative text is consistently near the top.

## Contrast: the numbers
WCAG uses a **contrast ratio** computed from the relative luminance of two colours, ranging from 1:1 (same colour) to 21:1 (black on white).

| Criterion | Level | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) | AA | Text 4.5:1; large text 3:1 |
| 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) | AAA | Text 7:1; large text 4.5:1 |
| 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast | AA | 3:1 for UI component boundaries and states (input borders, focus rings, checkbox outlines, toggle states) and meaningful graphics (chart lines, icons that carry meaning) |

"Large text" is at least 18 point (24 CSS px) regular, or 14 point (about 18.66 CSS px) bold. Exceptions: disabled controls, pure decoration, logos and text that is part of a photo.

Things people get wrong:
- **Placeholder text** at `#999` on white is about 2.8:1 and fails if it carries information.
- **Text over images and gradients**: contrast must hold at the worst point. Use a solid or semi-opaque scrim behind the text.
- **Hover, focus and disabled-looking states**: a button whose label goes from 4.6:1 to 3.5:1 on hover fails in that state.
- **Input borders** at `#ddd` on white (about 1.4:1) fail 1.4.11, so users with low vision cannot find the field.
- **Brand colours**: the classic mid-blue, orange or green on white often lands between 3:1 and 4.5:1. That works for large headings, not body text or small buttons.

The WCAG 2 contrast formula has known weaknesses (it treats some dark-mode pairs oddly and ignores font weight and size beyond the large-text threshold). APCA, a perceptual contrast algorithm, was explored for WCAG 3, but it is **not** part of any current standard. For compliance in 2026, measure with the WCAG 2 ratio.

### Building contrast into a design system
```css
:root {
  --bg: oklch(99% 0 0);
  --fg: oklch(20% 0.02 260);        /* body text, well above 7:1 on --bg */
  --muted: oklch(45% 0.02 260);     /* secondary text, check it stays >= 4.5:1 */
  --border-input: oklch(55% 0.02 260); /* >= 3:1 against --bg for 1.4.11 */
  --ring: oklch(55% 0.2 260);
}
```
Tokens with contrast verified once (and tested automatically per theme, including dark mode) beat case-by-case checks. Tools: WebAIM's contrast checker, Chrome DevTools' colour picker (shows the ratio and AA/AAA lines), and axe in CI.

### Forced colours and user preferences
Windows high-contrast themes activate the `forced-colors: active` media query: the browser replaces your colours with a small user palette. Background images and box shadows used as borders disappear. Use real borders and outlines (even transparent ones), use `currentColor` in SVG icons, and test with forced colours emulation in DevTools. Also respect `prefers-contrast: more` when you can offer a higher-contrast theme.

## Do not use colour alone (1.4.1, A)
About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of colour vision deficiency, most commonly red-green. And colour is invisible to screen readers.

```text
Bad                                 Better
----------------------------------  ----------------------------------------
Red border on invalid field         Red border + icon + "Enter a valid email"
Green / red dots for status         Dot + text label ("Healthy", "Down"),
                                     or distinct icon shapes
Links blue in body text, no         Underlined links (or 3:1 contrast with
underline                            surrounding text + underline on hover/focus)
Chart series by colour only         Direct labels, patterns or markers,
                                     plus a data table alternative
Required fields in red               "(required)" text or asterisk with legend
```
For charts, the strongest accessible pattern is: direct labels on lines, a visible legend with shapes as well as colours, sufficient 3:1 contrast for lines against the background, and the underlying data available as a table.

## Motion and animation
Large or parallax motion, zooming transitions and auto-playing carousels can trigger dizziness, nausea and migraines for people with vestibular disorders. Relevant criteria:
- **2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (A)**: nothing flashes more than three times in any one second (above defined size and brightness thresholds). This is a seizure safety rule, not a preference.
- **2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A)**: anything that moves, blinks or scrolls automatically for more than five seconds alongside other content (carousels, marquees, auto-updating tickers, background videos) needs a pause or stop control.
- **2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA)**: motion triggered by interaction can be disabled unless essential.

Operating systems expose a "reduce motion" setting, available in CSS and JS:
```css
.card {
  transition: transform 300ms ease, opacity 300ms ease;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card {
    transition: opacity 150ms linear; /* keep a gentle fade, drop movement */
  }
  .card:hover {
    transform: none;
  }
  html {
    scroll-behavior: auto; /* no smooth scrolling */
  }
}
```
```ts
const reduced = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
element.animate(
  reduced ? [{ opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1 }] : [{ transform: "translateY(16px)", opacity: 0 }, { transform: "none", opacity: 1 }],
  { duration: reduced ? 150 : 400, easing: "ease-out" },
);
```
"Reduced" does not mean "none". Opacity fades and colour changes are generally fine; large translations, zooms, parallax and spinning are what to remove. Some teams invert the default: no motion unless `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`. Josh Comeau's article on accessible animations with `prefers-reduced-motion` walks through this "motion as an enhancement" approach for React hooks too.

Auto-playing video: muted background videos still need a pause control if they play longer than five seconds; audio that plays automatically for more than three seconds needs a way to stop it or control its volume (1.4.2 Audio Control, A).

## Images and alternative text (1.1.1, A)
Alternative text is not a description of the picture; it is **the information or function the image provides in this context**. The W3C WAI images tutorial has an alt decision tree; the condensed version:

```text
Is the image inside a link or button with no other text?
   yes -> alt describes the DESTINATION or ACTION ("Home", "Search")
Does it contain text?
   yes -> alt contains the same text (or avoid images of text entirely)
Does it add information the surrounding text does not?
   yes -> short, specific description of that information
   no  -> decorative: alt="" (empty, not missing), or a CSS background
Is it complex (chart, diagram)?
   -> short alt + a longer description nearby or linked (data table, summary)
```
Practical rules:
- **Empty `alt=""` versus missing `alt`**: empty means "decorative, skip it". A missing attribute makes many screen readers fall back to reading the file name ("IMG underscore 4032 dot jpeg").
- **Do not start with "Image of"**; the role is already announced.
- **Keep it concise** and context-specific. The same product photo might be `alt="Navy wool coat, front view"` on a product page and `alt=""` in a cart line where the product name is already beside it.
- **Inline SVG icons**: decorative ones get `aria-hidden="true"`; meaningful standalone ones get `role="img"` and an `aria-label` (or a `title` element as the first child, with `aria-labelledby` for reliability).
- **Next.js `Image` and similar components** require an `alt` prop; pass an empty string deliberately for decorative images, not a placeholder like "image".
- **User-generated images**: let users add alt text (as Mastodon and many social platforms do) and default to an empty or generic alt rather than the file name. AI-generated alt text can help as a draft, but it describes pixels, not intent, so treat it as a suggestion the author can edit.

Images of text (1.4.5, AA) should be avoided: they do not reflow, resize cleanly, or respect user colour settings.

## Captions, transcripts and audio description
| Need | Criterion | What to provide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prerecorded video with audio | 1.2.2 Captions (A) | Synchronised captions including speaker changes and meaningful sounds ("[door slams]") |
| Live video with audio | 1.2.4 Captions (Live) (AA) | Real-time captions (human CART or high-quality automatic with correction) |
| Visual information in video not in the audio | 1.2.5 Audio Description (AA) | Narration of important visual content, or a script written so visuals are described in the main audio |
| Audio-only (podcasts) | 1.2.1 (A) | A transcript |
| Video-only | 1.2.1 (A) | A transcript or audio track describing it |

On the web, captions are typically WebVTT files attached with a `track` element (`kind="captions"`, `srclang`, `label`) inside `video`. Use a player whose controls are keyboard accessible and labelled, and which lets users toggle captions and adjust their size. Raw automatic captions often mangle names and technical terms; review them before publishing anything important. Transcripts also help search, skimming and people in noisy places.

## Trade-offs
- **Brand versus contrast**: offer a darker variant of the brand colour for text and keep the bright one for large surfaces and decoration.
- **Motion design**: motion helps orientation (where did this panel come from?), so do not remove it for everyone; reduce it for those who ask.
- **Alt text effort**: it is editorial work, not engineering. Engineering's job is to make providing it easy and mandatory (CMS fields, lint rules, review checklists).

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Checking contrast in the design file but not in implemented states (hover, disabled-looking, dark mode).
- Grey-on-grey secondary text everywhere because it "looks clean".
- `alt` filled with keywords for SEO.
- Decorative icon fonts read aloud as strange characters because they were not hidden.
- Carousels that auto-advance with no pause control, and pause buttons that are not keyboard reachable.
- Ignoring `prefers-reduced-motion` in JS-driven animations (Framer Motion and GSAP need explicit handling; Framer Motion has a reduced-motion configuration option).

Debugging: axe and Lighthouse flag contrast and missing alt. DevTools rendering panel can emulate `prefers-reduced-motion`, `forced-colors`, and vision deficiencies (blurred vision, protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, achromatopsia), which is a fast way to see colour-only meaning.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** the specific contrast ratios, the idea that colour cannot be the only signal, reduced-motion handling, and judgement about alt text. Designers and engineers are both expected to know 4.5:1 and 3:1.

**Model 60-second answer ("How do you handle colour and contrast accessibly?"):**
1. Text 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), UI component boundaries and meaningful graphics 3:1 (1.4.11), all states included.
2. Bake it into design tokens and test themes automatically, including dark mode.
3. Never colour alone: pair it with text, icons, patterns or underlines.
4. Survive forced-colours mode with real outlines and `currentColor`.
5. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; provide pause controls for anything auto-moving longer than five seconds.

**Follow-ups:** What makes good alt text? When is `alt=""` correct? How would you make a chart accessible? What does a captions workflow look like?
keyPoints: Text needs 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text); UI boundaries, focus rings and meaningful graphics need 3:1
Colour is never the only signal: pair it with text, icons, patterns or underlines
Respect prefers-reduced-motion by removing movement, not all feedback; pause anything auto-moving over 5 seconds
Alt text conveys the image's purpose in context; alt="" for decorative images, never a missing attribute
Prerecorded video needs captions (A) and audio description of important visuals (AA); audio needs transcripts
interview: What contrast ratios does WCAG require, and how do you build them into a design system?
How do you write good alt text, and when should alt be empty?
How do you respect users who are sensitive to motion?
Why should colour never be the only way to convey information, and how do you fix it?

check.q: A text input's border is #ddd on a white background (about 1.4:1). Which criterion does it fail?
options: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), because it is text
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, which needs 3:1 for UI component boundaries
2.4.7 Focus Visible
None; borders are decorative
check.why: The border is what identifies the control, so it needs 3:1 against adjacent colours under 1.4.11.

check.q: What is the correct alt for a decorative flourish image next to a heading?
options: alt="decorative flourish image"
Omit the alt attribute entirely
alt="" (empty) so screen readers skip it
alt="image"
check.why: Empty alt marks it decorative. Omitting alt can make screen readers read the file name.

check.q: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, what is the most sensible change to a card hover animation that lifts and scales the card?
options: Remove the movement and scale but keep a short opacity or colour change
Remove all hover feedback entirely
Make the animation slower
Nothing; reduced motion only applies to video
check.why: Reduced motion targets movement such as translation, zoom and parallax; subtle fades and colour changes remain useful feedback.

lessons.title: Accessible components: APG patterns and headless libraries
lessons.summary: The ARIA Authoring Practices contracts for disclosure, dialog, menu, tabs, combobox and tooltips, plus how to choose and wrap headless libraries like React Aria and Radix.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Most accessibility bugs in modern apps live in a handful of interactive components: dialogs, dropdown menus, comboboxes (autocomplete, select-with-search), tabs, accordions, tooltips, date pickers, data grids. Each has an expected **contract**: roles, states, and a keyboard model that screen reader and keyboard users already know from operating systems and other sites. The **ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)**, published by the W3C WAI, documents these contracts as "patterns" with working examples. It is not normative like WCAG, but it is the closest thing to a specification for widget behaviour, and libraries such as React Aria, Radix and Headless UI cite it. The APG itself warns that its examples are not production-ready, and that ARIA support varies across assistive tech; test before trusting. Two principles run through every pattern: 1. **Use native HTML first.** `details`/`summary` is a disclosure. `dialog` is a dialog. `select` is a listbox. The APG patterns are for when native elements cannot do the job. 2. **Do not invent your own keyboard model.** Users expect the APG one: arrow keys in composites, Escape to dismiss, Home/End to jump, type-ahead in lists. ## Disclosure (show/hide) The simplest pattern and the one you should reach for most often: FAQ answers, "show more", collapsible sidebar sections, and even most "dropdown" navigation menus. ```text button [aria-expanded=false, aria-controls=panel] --Enter/Space--> toggles div#panel [hidden] ``` ```tsx // Native, zero JS: announced as a disclosure/summary with expanded state
Shipping and returns

Free returns within 30 days.

``` Use the button version (see the semantics lesson) when you need animation control or custom layout. A site navigation "dropdown" is usually best as a disclosure of links, **not** an ARIA `menu`: Tab moves through the links naturally, and screen readers stay in their normal browse mode. ## Dialog (modal) | Requirement | Detail | | --- | --- | | Role and name | `role="dialog"` (native `dialog` has it), `aria-modal="true"` for custom ones, named by `aria-labelledby` pointing at the title; optional `aria-describedby` for a short message | | Focus on open | First focusable element, or the least destructive action, or the title (with `tabindex=-1`) when content is long | | While open | Tab and Shift+Tab cycle within; background inert; Escape closes | | On close | Focus returns to the invoking element (or a logical fallback) | | Variant | `role="alertdialog"` for urgent confirmations ("Discard changes?") | As covered in the keyboard lesson, `HTMLDialogElement.showModal()` gives you top layer rendering, inert background, Escape handling and focus restoration. The remaining work is naming, initial focus choice, and scroll locking of the page behind. ## Menu button and menu The ARIA `menu` role means an **application-style menu**: like a desktop app's File menu or a "More actions" kebab menu, containing commands. ```text
  • Rename
  • Duplicate
  • Delete
Keyboard: Enter/Space/Down on button opens and focuses first item; Up opens and focuses last. Inside: Up/Down move (wrapping), Home/End, type a character to jump, Enter activates and closes, Escape closes and returns focus to the button. Tab closes the menu and moves on. ``` Notes: - `menuitemcheckbox` and `menuitemradio` for toggles inside menus, with `aria-checked`. - Screen readers switch to focus/application handling inside menus, so arbitrary content (forms, paragraphs, links mixed with buttons) does not belong in them. - Do not put the `menu` role on site navigation. It changes how screen readers present the content and promises arrow-key behaviour. ## Tabs ```text
...
...
``` - The tab list is one Tab stop (roving tabindex); Left/Right arrows move between tabs (Up/Down for vertical tab lists, set `aria-orientation="vertical"`); Home/End go to first and last. - **Automatic activation**: arrowing to a tab shows its panel immediately. Good when panels render instantly. - **Manual activation**: arrows move focus, Enter or Space activates. Use when showing a panel is expensive (network fetch), to avoid loading every panel the user passes. - The panel gets `tabindex="0"` when it contains no focusable content, so keyboard users can reach and scroll it. - If the "tabs" change the URL and load different pages, they are navigation: use links with `aria-current="page"`, not the tab pattern. ## Combobox The hardest common widget, and the one most often built badly. An input whose value can be chosen from a popup (usually a listbox). ```text input role=combobox aria-expanded=true|false aria-controls=listbox-id aria-autocomplete="list" (suggestions filter as you type) aria-activedescendant=opt-3 (the option highlighted, while DOM focus stays in input) ul role=listbox id=listbox-id li role=option id=opt-3 aria-selected=true Keys (in the input): Down open popup / move to next option Up previous option Enter accept highlighted option, close Escape close popup (second Escape may clear the input) Alt+Down open without moving typing filters; DOM focus never leaves the input Also: announce result counts politely ("5 suggestions"), and the highlighted option must scroll into view. ``` Why `aria-activedescendant`: the user must keep typing, so real focus has to stay in the input. The screen reader reads the option referenced by `aria-activedescendant` as if it were focused. ARIA 1.2 simplified the combobox pattern (the role goes on the input itself); older 1.0/1.1 implementations used wrapper elements and still exist in legacy libraries. Before building one, ask whether you need it: - A `select` covers short, fixed lists and is excellent on mobile. - `input` with a `datalist` gives native suggestions (limited styling, inconsistent support across screen reader pairings, but zero code). - Browsers are rolling out the customisable `select` (`appearance: base-select`), which allows styling the native control; check current support before relying on it. ## Tooltips A tooltip is a short, non-interactive description shown on hover **and focus**. The ARIA `tooltip` role exists but is loosely supported; the robust approach is `aria-describedby` from the trigger to the tooltip text. WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (AA) requires that such content is **dismissible** (Escape without moving the pointer), **hoverable** (the pointer can move onto it without it disappearing) and **persistent** (stays until dismissed or no longer relevant). Never put essential information or interactive content (links, buttons) in a tooltip; that is a popover or dialog. Touch screens have no hover at all. ## Headless libraries: build or buy Implementing these patterns correctly across browsers, screen readers, touch devices, RTL languages, and virtual keyboards is months of specialist work. Headless libraries give you behaviour and ARIA with your own styling: | Library | Model | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | React Aria (Adobe) | Hooks (`useComboBox`, `useDialog`) plus React Aria Components | Most rigorous: extensive screen reader and touch testing, internationalisation, the basis of Adobe's Spectrum | | Radix Primitives | Unstyled components (`Dialog`, `DropdownMenu`, `Tabs`) | Popular through shadcn/ui; follows APG patterns, good focus management | | Headless UI (Tailwind Labs) | Unstyled components for React and Vue | Smaller set, simple API | | Ariakit | Low-level composable primitives | Fine-grained control, strong focus on correctness | | Native platform | `dialog`, `details`, `popover`, `select` | Free, improving every year; check support matrices | Trade-offs to articulate: - **Buy** when you need comboboxes, menus, date pickers or grids. The library authors have already hit the VoiceOver-on-iOS bugs you have not discovered yet. - **But a library is not a guarantee.** You can still break it: passing no label to a `Dialog.Title`, wrapping triggers in extra `div`s, overriding focus behaviour, or styling focus rings away. Libraries also differ in which screen readers they test. - **Build** simple things (disclosure, toggle button) from native elements; the code is short and you avoid a dependency. - **Lock the API**: your design system's wrapper should require an accessible name (`label` prop typed as required) and forbid props that break the pattern. ## Example: a design-system Dialog wrapper on Radix ```tsx import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog"; type ModalProps = { title: string; // required: becomes the accessible name description?: string; trigger: React.ReactElement; children: React.ReactNode; }; export function Modal({ title, description, trigger, children }: ModalProps) { return ( {trigger} {title} {description ? {description} : null} {children} ); } ``` Radix handles focus trapping, Escape, returning focus to the trigger and hiding the rest of the app from assistive tech; the wrapper guarantees a title and a labelled close button. `asChild` keeps the consumer's button as the actual trigger element rather than nesting a button inside a button. ## Common mistakes - ARIA `menu` for site navigation; `role="listbox"` without `aria-selected` or keyboard support. - Tabs implemented as links that also have `role="tab"` and change the URL. - Combobox where DOM focus jumps into the list, so typing stops working; or `aria-activedescendant` pointing to an id that is not rendered. - Tooltips holding essential text, or disappearing when the pointer moves towards them. - Accordions using headings as buttons (`h3 onClick`), instead of a button inside the heading. - Nested interactive elements (a button inside a link, a link inside a summary) which produce undefined behaviour. - Assuming a headless library made the component accessible without ever testing it with a screen reader. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you know the APG exists and can describe the contract for at least dialog, tabs and combobox, and whether you can make a reasoned build-versus-buy call. Senior candidates may be asked to design a design-system component API that makes accessibility the default. **Model 60-second answer ("How would you build an accessible combobox?"):** 1. First check whether `select` or `datalist` is enough; if not, use a tested library such as React Aria. 2. Input gets `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `aria-autocomplete`; popup is a `listbox` of `option`s. 3. DOM focus stays in the input; `aria-activedescendant` points to the highlighted option, which scrolls into view. 4. Keys: Down/Up move, Enter selects, Escape closes; announce result counts politely. 5. Test with NVDA, JAWS if possible, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, because support differs. **Follow-ups:** Disclosure versus menu for a nav dropdown? Automatic versus manual tab activation? Radix versus React Aria? How do tooltips satisfy 1.4.13?
keyPoints: The APG documents the expected roles, states and keyboard model for each widget; follow it rather than inventing one
Prefer native details, dialog, select and popover before custom ARIA widgets
Site navigation dropdowns are disclosures of links, not ARIA menus
Comboboxes keep DOM focus in the input and point aria-activedescendant at the highlighted option
Headless libraries handle the hard parts, but wrappers must require names and you must still test with screen readers

options: On each option in turn
On the listbox container
On the document body
In the input, with aria-activedescendant referencing the highlighted option
check.why: The user must keep typing, so focus stays in the input and aria-activedescendant tells AT which option is active.

check.q: When is manual tab activation (arrows move focus, Enter activates) preferable to automatic activation?
options: When showing a panel is expensive, such as requiring a network request
When there are fewer than three tabs
When tabs are vertical
Never; APG forbids manual activation
check.why: Automatic activation loads every panel the user arrows past; manual activation avoids that cost.

check.q: Which requirement does WCAG 1.4.13 place on tooltip-like content shown on hover or focus?
options: It must contain a close button
It must use role="tooltip"
It must be dismissible, hoverable and persistent
It must appear after a 500 ms delay
check.why: Users must be able to dismiss it without moving the pointer, move the pointer over it, and have it stay until dismissed.

projects.title: Accessible React UI kit with automated and screen reader verified components
projects.summary: A small design-system component library (button, dialog, menu button, tabs, combobox, disclosure, toast, form fields) that meets WCAG 2.2 AA, with typed APIs that make inaccessible usage hard, axe and keyboard tests in CI, and a published screen reader test matrix.
projects.why: Almost every frontend team has accessibility debt in its components, and few candidates can show they know how to fix it at the source. This project proves you can implement APG keyboard models, manage focus, announce dynamic changes, design token-level contrast, and build a testing pipeline that keeps it all from regressing. It also gives you concrete stories for senior interview questions about design systems, component API design and engineering process.
projects.architecture:
```text
packages/
  tokens/        colours (contrast-checked pairs), spacing, focus ring, motion
                 -> build step verifies every text/background pair >= 4.5:1
  ui/            components
    Button, IconButton (label: string required)
    Field (label, hint, error -> id wiring + aria-invalid)
    Dialog, AlertDialog (native dialog or Radix)
    MenuButton, Tabs, Combobox (React Aria hooks)
    Disclosure, Toaster + useAnnounce (global live regions)
  docs/          Storybook: stories per state, a11y addon, keyboard tables

CI: tsc -> eslint (jsx-a11y) -> vitest (role queries + axe)
    -> storybook test runner (axe per story, light/dark/forced colours)
    -> playwright (keyboard journeys + axe on open states) -> publish
Manual: screen reader matrix (NVDA+Firefox, VoiceOver+Safari macOS/iOS,
        TalkBack+Chrome) recorded per component release
```
Key decisions: lean on a headless library for the hard widgets instead of re-implementing them; make accessible names required in the TypeScript API; one app-level announcer instead of ad-hoc live regions; contrast enforced at the token layer; every component documented with its keyboard model and the APG pattern it follows.

deepDives.title: Making accessibility the default through the component API
Focus management rules across the kit
deepDives.body:
Focus loss is the bug that automated tools never find. The kit defines a small set of rules and implements each once.

```text
Event                         Focus goes to
----------------------------  ----------------------------------------
Dialog opens                  initial focus prop, else first focusable,
                              else the dialog title (tabindex=-1)
Dialog closes                 the trigger; if unmounted, a fallback ref
Menu item activated           back to the menu button
Toast appears                 nowhere (announced instead)
List item deleted             next item, else previous, else list heading
Form submit fails             error summary (or first invalid field)
```

The dialog uses `showModal()` (or Radix, which makes the rest of the page unreachable for assistive tech and traps focus). For the deletion rule, the list component keeps refs to items and computes the next target before removing the item, because once React unmounts the focused node, `document.activeElement` becomes `body` and the user is lost at the top of the page.

Testing: Playwright journeys assert `toBeFocused()` after each event. These tests caught more real bugs than any axe rule.

deepDives.title: Why one global announcer instead of live regions per component
deepDives.body:
Early versions had each component render its own `aria-live` region. Three problems showed up in the NVDA speech viewer log:

1. **Missed announcements**: regions mounted together with their first message were never registered, so the first toast was silent.
2. **Duplicates**: the combobox and a page-level results count both announced "5 results".
3. **Contention**: several assertive regions competed and cut each other off.

The fix is a single pair of regions (polite and assertive) mounted at the app root, exposed through `useAnnounce(message, priority)`. Messages are cleared and re-set after a short delay so identical repeats are spoken, and high-frequency sources (typing in a combobox) are debounced before announcing. Components that need structured live content, like a chat `log`, keep their own region because that region is the content itself.

The cost is coupling: the kit requires an `AnnouncerProvider` at the root. Missing providers fall back to a no-op with a development warning.
